# M3.1 startup recipe lifecycle research

Researched on 22 September 2026 (host-local date). Target: ATM10 8.2, Minecraft 1.21.1, NeoForge 21.1.251, Java 21. This is a diagnosis of the user's M3 integrated-server failure, based on read-only log, source and exact installed JAR inspection. The research did not issue game commands, interact with the UI, modify the installed instance, or access player saves. Build and repaired-runtime results belong in the separate verification report.

## Observed failure

The user's installed M3 0.3.0 reported generation 1 as failed during selection, after visiting **487 of 93,096 definitions in one slice**, with zero normalized definitions. Its message was `Recipe manager, definition table or count changed during indexing; awaiting completed datapack reload`. Later planning commands continued to reject that generation.

This is not evidence that the game supplied an invalid recipe. The guard found that the recipe source was no longer the source with which that index job began. Rejecting that partial index was correct; remaining unavailable indefinitely after a legitimate recipe update was the Companion defect.

Only relevant recipe-lifecycle entries were inspected from the installed instance's `logs/latest.log`. The following references use the line numbers present at inspection, not stable IDs; this file is mutable and rotates between launches. No unrelated chat, player identity, address, credentials, or world data is reproduced here.

| Local log reference | Observed fact |
| --- | --- |
| Line 21989, 22:07:58.054 | The recipe manager initially reports 92,921 loaded recipes. |
| Line 22636, 22:08:06.994 | The integrated Minecraft 1.21.1 server starts. |
| Line 22670, 22:08:14.802 | KubeJS reports its server resource reload complete. |
| Lines 22694–22696, 22:08:24.175 | Potions Master registers 44 dynamic recipes at server start. |
| Lines 22801–22849, 22:09:13.378–22:09:14.627 | Ars Unification logs twelve recipe processors followed by `Finished processing recipes in 1.449 s`. |
| Lines 24099–24101, 22:13:18.531–22:13:18.547 | Companion reports the failed generation and 487/93,096 selection progress. |
| Lines 24178–24180, 22:16:32.841–22:16:32.842 | The same failed generation remains unavailable. |

The initial recipe count and the index's captured total differ by 175. The earlier isolated production-server smoke log similarly reports 95,054 loaded recipes and an index of 95,229 definitions, also a difference of 175. These count differences are observations; they do not identify every mod that generated those recipes.

## Exact late replacement mechanism

The installed `ars_unification-1.2.21.jar` has SHA-256 `9c15dd133f4973fe7f60064d74b0b09f0bfe3cc8d87d593ce7bc5b66503f6c33`. Its classes were inspected directly with the installed Java 21 `javap -c -p`, and annotation metadata with `javap -v -p`.

`dev.qther.ars_unification.ArsUnification.onDatapackSync(OnDatapackSyncEvent)` is annotated `@SubscribeEvent(priority = EventPriority.LOWEST)`. Its branch calls `processRecipes(server)` when either:

- The event player is null, meaning a sync for all players; or
- Its static `processorsRegistered` flag is false, including the first joining-player sync in the process.

`processRecipes` first checks that the mod's server configuration is loaded, initializes/sorts enabled processors, and invokes their `processRecipes()` methods. The matching processor names and completion message appear in the user's log.

`dev.qther.ars_unification.processors.Processor.processRecipes()` copies the current recipe-manager `byName` map into an `Object2ObjectOpenHashMap`, adds its derived recipe holders, then **unconditionally calls `RecipeManager.replaceRecipes(map.values())`**. The call is at bytecode offset 454. Even a pass that adds no entries replaces the table, so a same-count replacement remains a real generation change. Companion must not disable table-identity validation merely because the count stays unchanged.

The accessor used by Ars Unification is part of that mod; Companion does not need to link to it, reflect into it, or integrate with that mod by name. Generic lifecycle recovery should cover the actual table replacement.

## NeoForge event ordering

The exact source archive is `build/moddev/artifacts/neoforge-21.1.251-sources.jar`, produced by the pinned build with official Mojang mappings. Relevant entries are `net/neoforged/neoforge/event/OnDatapackSyncEvent.java` and `net/minecraft/server/players/PlayerList.java`.

The event documentation says it fires when a player joins or the reload command runs, before tags and crafting recipes are sent to the client. `PlayerList.placeNewPlayer` posts `OnDatapackSyncEvent(this, joiningPlayer)` before constructing/sending the recipe update packet. `PlayerList.reloadResources` posts `OnDatapackSyncEvent(this, null)` before broadcasting tags and recipes.

M3's `RuntimeKnowledge.datapacksSynced` ignores every non-null player event. On a null event, it immediately captures the source table from a default-priority listener. Therefore:

1. A first-player sync can legitimately mutate recipes after the initial server-start index has begun, without scheduling another Companion build.
2. During a null reload sync, a later `LOWEST` listener can replace the table after Companion captures it, invalidating the newly scheduled generation too.
3. Treating event notification as a guarantee that every listener has finished is unsafe. A listener at `LOWEST` is also insufficient as a general ordering guarantee because other listeners may have the same priority or perform later work.

The earlier M2 research correctly said that a joining-player event alone is not proof of a new recipe generation. The M3.1 correction is that it is also **not proof of an unchanged generation**. Capture after event dispatch and direct freshness checks are required.

## Why the dedicated smoke passed

The isolated production-server smoke used a synthetic player without a real `PlayerList.placeNewPlayer` login. Its log contains Ars Unification loading/configuration messages but none of the processor/completion messages observed in the user's log. Its index completed against the pre-login recipe table.

The inspected bytecode, source ordering and user log form a strong causal explanation for the failure. The old diagnostic did not record which freshness predicate changed or a before/after count, so it cannot independently prove that no second mod changed the table in the same interval. The confirmed Ars Unification replacements are sufficient to invalidate the captured table.

This is a **first-player recipe-sync coverage gap**, not an intrinsically client-only or integrated-server-only defect. A dedicated server's first real player login can exercise the same handler. The old smoke result remains valid within its pre-login scope and cannot certify this missing lifecycle path.

## Recovery requirements derived from the evidence

- Keep manager identity, definition-table identity and count checks. Never expose the abandoned partial generation or a stale previously ready index.
- Treat lifecycle notifications as signals. Capture the replacement source on a later logical-server tick after synchronous event listeners finish; coalesce repeated signals.
- Check joining-player syncs without rebuilding a genuinely unchanged ready index on every login.
- Recover from observed table changes without requiring the player to reload the whole pack. Keep automatic retries finite and time-sliced; continuously changing data must reach an explicit unavailable/backoff state rather than an endless rebuild loop.
- Verify freshness again before publishing a completed job, because a recipe callback can replace the table during an extraction slice.
- Differentiate a recoverable stale-generation condition from unrelated programmer/API failures. Do not suppress arbitrary `IllegalStateException` failures merely because a command normally sees a building/unavailable index.
- Test null and non-null sync events with a later-priority same-count replacement, changes during a slice, unchanged joins, coalesced signals, continuous mutations, failure propagation, and stop/reload cleanup.

No recovery behavior or repaired actual-ATM10 result is claimed by this research document. The independent M3.1 adversarial review records the final implementation and the evidence actually available after the patch.
